A brass hinge on the cellar door
Where does this narrow path lead?
Close the gate behind you.
Salt water rises in the harbour.
Two crows on a wet fence
Why is the ferry running late?
Bring the ladder around the back.
Mountain air thins above the treeline.
A small bakery near the river
Has the letter arrived yet?
Please wait outside the reading room.
The bridge carries traffic in one direction.
Dry grass along the railway embankment
Who left the lantern burning?
Count the chairs before locking up.
Rain softened the clay road overnight.
An old copper coin, badly worn
Is the well water safe?
Turn left at the stone marker.
Fog settles in the valley each morning.
The last train of the evening
How deep is this lake?
Hold the rope with both hands!
Bees moved slowly in the cold.
A cracked bell in the tower
Did anyone find the missing key?
Boil the water for ten minutes.
Sand covered the tiles by noon.
Three lamps along a quiet street
Can the roof hold this snow?
Sign the register at the desk.
Wind bent the young pines eastward.
A ledger bound in green cloth
What time does the market open?
Leave the parcel with the porter.
Ice formed on the shallow pond.
The smell of wet stone
Should we take the coastal road?
Measure twice before cutting the plank.
Sunlight warmed the empty courtyard.
A rope ladder, frayed at the top
Which door leads to the garden?
Keep the flour in a dry place.
The tide left shells on the sand.
One candle burning in the hall
Are the shutters closed for winter?
Follow the stream until it widens.
Frost cracked the shallow drain.
A heavy door with iron studs
Does this clock keep good time?
Water the seedlings before dusk.
The bread cooled on a wire rack.
Cold ash in the grate
Have they repaired the sea wall?
Sharpen the blade against the stone.
A thin mist over the fields
Is the mill still grinding?
Store the nets under the bench.
Sheep crossed the road without hurry.
Broken glass beside the gate
When does the harvest begin?
Lock the shed and come inside!
The lighthouse beam swept the bay slowly.

The footbridge over the canal is built of riveted iron and painted a dull green. Each morning someone crosses it with two dogs, and the boards ring under their feet. By noon the paint is warm enough to give off a faint smell of tar.

To start the old kiln you open the lower vent, lay a bed of dry kindling, and wait until the draught pulls steadily upward. Only then does the coal go in, a shovelful at a time. Loading it too early smothers the fire and wastes an hour.

The reading room occupies the top floor and has eleven tall windows facing north. Dust hangs in the light above the long tables. Readers speak in half voices, and the loudest sound most afternoons is a chair being dragged across the boards.

She keeps her tools in a wooden box with a sliding lid, arranged so that the handles all point the same way. When a chisel comes back dull she sharpens it that evening rather than the next morning, because a dull edge slips and cuts the hand holding the wood.

The river narrows below the mill and runs fast over a shelf of grey stone. In dry months the shelf stands clear of the water and children walk across it. After heavy rain the whole channel turns brown and carries branches down toward the lower bridge.

Bread is mixed at four, shaped at six, and in the oven before the first customers arrive. The baker judges the proof by pressing a thumb into the dough and watching how slowly the dent fills. Nothing in the process is timed by a clock alone.

The station platform is longer than the trains that use it, so the far end is overgrown with grass between the slabs. A wooden shelter stands there with its bench intact and its roof half gone. Nobody waits at that end any more.

He learned to repair nets from an older neighbour who worked without looking at his hands. The trick, he was told, is to keep the tension even; a tight mesh beside a loose one tears first. It took a winter before his own repairs stopped showing.

The hill behind the village is bare on its south side and wooded on the north. Sheep have cut narrow terraces across the bare slope over many decades, and from the valley these look like contour lines drawn on the grass.

Every spring the school repaints the fence around the yard. The children are given the lower boards and the caretaker takes the rest. The result is a band of uneven colour at knee height that nobody has ever suggested correcting.

The market opens at dawn under a roof of corrugated sheets. Water from the fish stalls runs along a shallow channel in the floor toward a drain at the far corner. By ten the stone is dry again and the traders are folding their tables.

A low wall of dry stone separates the orchard from the road. It has no mortar, and its stability comes entirely from how the stones were fitted. When a section falls, rebuilding it is a matter of sorting the stones by shape before laying a single one.

The lighthouse keeper's cottage now holds weather instruments and nothing else. Its walls are three courses thick and the windows are small. Even in a gale the rooms are quiet, which visitors find stranger than the noise outside.

She walks the same route each evening: down the lane, along the field edge, and back by the churchyard. The distance is a little over three kilometres. She says the value is not the exercise but that the route requires no decisions.

Copper turns green outdoors, and the roof of the courthouse has been that colour longer than anyone living remembers it being brown. The gutters, replaced more recently, are still dark and bright, which makes the roof look older than it is.

The bee shed stands at the top of the garden, facing away from the prevailing wind. Ten hives sit on a low platform of concrete blocks. In cold weather you can hold a hand against the wood and feel a faint warmth through it.

Coffee is roasted in small batches in a drum turned by hand. The roaster listens for the first sharp cracking of the beans and then counts, because after that point a difference of thirty seconds changes the taste of the whole batch.

The tunnel under the ridge is lined with brick for most of its length but cut straight into rock in the middle section. Water seeps through there and freezes in winter, so the crew inspects that stretch twice as often as the rest.

Their kitchen table came from a farmhouse sale and is too large for the room. Two of the chairs must be pulled out before anyone can reach the window. Nobody has proposed selling it, and it has now been there eleven years.

The path to the summit crosses three fences by means of wooden stiles. The last one leans badly and shakes when weight is put on it. Walkers step over the wall beside it instead, and the grass there is worn bare.

Salt is harvested from shallow pans that are filled at high tide and then sealed. Evaporation does the rest over several weeks. The crust is raked by hand into low ridges, left to drain, and carried up the bank in flat baskets.

The clock on the town hall runs about four minutes fast, and has for as long as anyone bothers to recall. Shopkeepers set their watches by it anyway and simply subtract. A visitor once corrected it and was asked politely to change it back.

He grinds the lenses on a rotating plate charged with fine abrasive, checking the curve against a metal gauge every few minutes. The final polishing takes longer than all the shaping before it and cannot be hurried without leaving faint circular marks.

Rain came in from the west all afternoon and the yard flooded to a depth of a few centimetres. By evening the water had drained away through the gravel, leaving a fan of silt across the lower half of the concrete.

The library keeps its older maps in flat drawers, one sheet to a drawer, separated by tissue. Handling them requires two people because the paper is brittle at the folds. Most requests are answered with a photograph rather than the original.

In the workshop the floor slopes very slightly toward the door so that spilled water leaves on its own. The slope is not visible, but a dropped pencil always rolls the same way, which newcomers notice within a day or two.

Geese cross the valley twice a year, always along the same line of hills. They fly lower in poor weather and can be heard before they are seen. Farmers there use their passage to mark the beginning and the end of the cold season.

The bakery's front window has a shallow shelf where loaves are stacked in the morning. Heat from them fogs the glass, and by the time the fog clears the shelf is usually empty. In wet weather the effect lasts most of the day.

She sorts the seed by hand on a tray with a raised rim, tipping it back and forth so that the lighter husks gather at one end. Machines do this faster, but her method loses less of the good seed and she has never seen a reason to change.

The quarry closed long ago and the pit has filled with green water. Its walls show clear horizontal bands where different layers were cut. Swimming is forbidden, mainly because the water is far colder a metre down than it appears from the rim.

A narrow staircase runs from the shop up to two rooms that were once storage. The treads are worn into shallow hollows near the wall side, which is where people naturally place their feet when carrying something in both hands.

The blacksmith heats the bar until it is bright orange, works it for perhaps forty seconds, and returns it to the fire. Most of the day is spent waiting. The actual shaping, added together, would take less than an hour.

Fog settles in the low field on clear nights and lifts by the middle of the morning. From the ridge above, the field looks like a white lake with the tops of fence posts showing. It never spreads to the field on the other side of the lane.

Their neighbour keeps a weather record in a hard-backed notebook, one line each day: temperature at eight, rainfall, wind direction, and a short remark. The notebooks go back several decades and are stored in order on a shelf above the stove.

The pier is repaired in sections during the winter, when the tide is lowest at midday. Each replaced plank is a shade lighter than its neighbours for about a year. The pattern of light and dark records the order of every repair.

Grapes are picked into small crates rather than large ones so the weight of the fruit does not crush the lower layers. The crates are stacked on a trailer four high and driven slowly, because a sudden stop bruises more fruit than a whole hot afternoon.

The corridor between the two wings has a glass roof and is noticeably warmer than either building. Staff use it as a place to eat when the weather is poor. In summer nobody goes there at all except to pass through quickly.

He repaints the boat every second spring, scraping the old coat back to bare wood along the waterline where it fails first. Above that line the paint holds for years. The work takes eight days and he starts as soon as the frost ends.

The road up the pass has eleven hairpin bends, each with a stone marker on the outside edge. Snow closes the top section for several months, and the markers are then the only way to see where the road runs beneath the drifts.

Wool is washed twice, first in warm water and then in cool, and laid out on netting frames to dry. Drying indoors takes three days; outdoors on a windy afternoon it takes one. The colour of the finished fleece depends heavily on which was used.

A row of poplars was planted along the drive to break the wind. They grew faster than expected and now shade the house until late morning. Removing one would help, but the row looks wrong with a gap and the question is raised every year.

The cellar stays near twelve degrees all year without any equipment, because it is cut into the hillside and has only one small vent. Bottles stored there for a decade show no change. The floor is compacted earth and is swept, never washed.

Boats are hauled out by a chain that runs from a winch at the top of the slip. The chain is heavy enough that two people are needed to carry the free end down to the water, and the descent is slower than the hauling.

She teaches beginners to throw pots by having them centre the same lump of clay ten times before shaping anything. Most find this tedious and several give up, but those who continue rarely have trouble with the wall thickness later.

The bell in the small tower is rung by hand and has a rope that hangs almost to the floor. Ringing it well is a matter of rhythm rather than strength. A visitor pulling hard produces a flat, uneven sound that carries much less far.

Wind turbines on the far ridge turn slowly enough to count the blades from the valley floor. On still days they stop entirely and the ridge looks bare. Their shadows sweep across the fields in the early evening in long, regular passes.

The stove is fed with split beech that has dried under cover for two summers. Wood dried for only one season burns unevenly and coats the flue. Cleaning the flue takes an afternoon and is the only maintenance the whole system needs.

A colony of swifts nests under the eaves of the granary each year and leaves again before the end of the warm season. The owners have delayed reroofing three times on their account. The birds return to the same gaps, apparently without difficulty.

The high street bends twice, following a stream that was covered over long before the present buildings went up. Cellars along that line are damp, and one shop keeps its stock on pallets rather than the floor for exactly that reason.

Cheese is turned in the store once a week, each wheel lifted and set down on its other face. This keeps the moisture even. Missing a turn is not serious; missing four in a row shows as a soft band around the middle of the wheel.

The old tram rails are still visible in two places where the asphalt has worn thin. Cyclists know to cross them at an angle. The rest of the line was lifted for scrap, and its route now survives mainly as an unusually straight row of trees.

Their well is lined with brick to a depth of about nine metres and has never gone dry, though the level drops noticeably in a long summer. A bucket dropped in takes just over a second to strike the water when the level is high.

He cleans the printing type by hand after every run, letter by letter, using a stiff brush and a solvent that evaporates fast. Ink left overnight hardens in the counters and dulls the impression, and no amount of later cleaning brings the face back fully.

The valley floor is flat enough for the road to run straight for six kilometres. Drivers speed there and the local council has placed a line of low barriers to break the view ahead. Whether this helps is disputed at every meeting.

Herons stand in the shallows below the weir at first light and leave once the mist clears. They do not tolerate anyone approaching within about thirty paces. From the far bank you can watch them for an hour without disturbing anything.

The stone floor of the entrance hall is laid in a simple pattern of squares set on the diagonal. Two tiles near the door are replacements and are slightly bluer than the rest. Everyone who has worked there for a while stops noticing them.

Sheets of glass are cut on a padded bench with a wheeled tool drawn once along a straightedge. A second pass never improves the cut and usually ruins it. The sheet is then tapped from underneath and separates along the score with a dry click.

The allotments are divided by paths of trodden ash. Each plot has a shed of some kind, none of them alike, and several built from doors and window frames taken from demolished houses. Water comes from four standpipes shared among about forty plots.

In late summer the reservoir drops far enough to expose the foundations of a farm that stood in the valley before the dam. Visitors walk out over the cracked mud to look. Two weeks of rain covers everything again until the following year.

She takes the same seat on the bus, third from the front on the left, because the heater there works and the window opens. If it is taken she stands rather than sit elsewhere, which her colleagues find funnier than she does.

The chalk cliff retreats by a small amount every winter, and the coastal path has been moved inland four times. Old sections end abruptly at the edge. A fence marks the current line, set back far enough to last perhaps another decade.

Timber for the roof was cut on site and left stacked with spacers between the boards for a full year. Building with green wood would have been faster, but the frame would have twisted as it dried and every joint would have opened.

The cat sleeps on the warm cover of the pump housing in the yard and moves only when the pump starts. It has learned the sound that comes just before, and is usually off the cover a second or two ahead of the vibration.

Snow on the north-facing roof lasts about a week longer than on the south side, so from the road one slope is white and the other wet and dark. Meltwater from the south side freezes overnight in the gutter and has twice torn it loose.

A glacier moves because the weight of accumulated ice deforms the crystals in its interior, so the whole mass creeps downhill at a rate usually measured in metres per year. Where the bed is wet, meltwater lubricates the contact and the ice slides as well as deforms, which makes such glaciers noticeably faster than cold ones frozen to the rock beneath them. The moving ice carries rock fragments of every size, and these grind the valley floor into the broad rounded trough that survives long after the ice has gone. Ridges of unsorted debris left along the margins mark the furthest advance, and they are read as a record of the climate that once fed the glacier.

Bread dough rises because yeast consumes the simple sugars released as enzymes break down the starch in flour, and the carbon dioxide it produces is trapped by an elastic network of gluten proteins. Kneading aligns those proteins and encourages them to bond, which is why a well worked dough holds gas that a slack one would lose. A long, cool fermentation gives bacteria time to produce acids alongside the gas, and these contribute much of the flavour that a hurried rise never develops. In the oven the trapped bubbles expand, the yeast dies, and the starch sets into a permanent foam whose walls stiffen as water leaves the crust.

A suspension bridge carries its deck on hangers dropped from two main cables, and those cables run over the tops of tall towers to anchorages buried in rock or concrete on either bank. The cables work purely in tension, taking the load as a curve that deepens under weight, while the towers pass the vertical component of that pull down to their foundations. Because the deck itself carries almost no load along its length, it can be slender, which is why early designs proved dangerously sensitive to wind. Modern decks are therefore stiffened with trusses or shaped like an aerofoil so that moving air cannot drive them into a growing oscillation.

A honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers returns to the hive and performs a repeated movement on the vertical comb that encodes where the patch lies. The angle of the straight portion relative to gravity corresponds to the angle of the food source relative to the sun, and the duration of that portion increases with distance. Bees crowding around the dancer touch her with their antennae, pick up the scent of the flowers she visited, and leave to search in the indicated direction. Because many foragers dance at once, the hive continually reallocates its workforce toward whichever patches are currently yielding the most nectar.

The optical heart of a traditional lighthouse is a lens built as a series of concentric rings rather than a single thick piece of glass, which keeps the assembly light enough to rotate and cheap enough to cast. Each ring bends light from the central lamp by a slightly different amount, and the outermost rings work partly by internal reflection, so that rays leaving in almost every direction are gathered into a narrow horizontal beam. As the assembly turns on its bearing, that beam sweeps the horizon and an observer sees a flash whenever it passes. The interval and grouping of the flashes differ from station to station, allowing a navigator to identify which light is in view.

Tides arise because the gravitational pull of the moon is stronger on the near side of the earth than on the far side, which stretches the ocean into two bulges that the planet then rotates beneath. The sun produces a smaller effect of the same kind, and when the two align the ranges are large, while at right angles they partly cancel and the ranges shrink. What a particular coast experiences, however, depends far more on the shape of its basin than on the astronomy, since a bay whose natural period of sloshing matches the driving rhythm can amplify the rise enormously. Narrow estuaries and shallow shelves therefore show ranges many times greater than the open ocean.

Paper is made from a dilute suspension of cellulose fibres that have been beaten in water until their surfaces fray into fine threads. A screen is dipped into the suspension and lifted, and as the water drains the fibres settle into a mat with their long axes lying roughly in the plane of the sheet. Pressing removes more water and brings the frayed surfaces into intimate contact, so that when drying pulls the last water out, hydrogen bonds form directly between fibres and hold the sheet together without any adhesive. A surface treatment is often added afterwards to slow the spread of ink, which would otherwise wick along the fibres and blur every line.

Bacterial populations acquire resistance to a drug in two distinct ways, and the difference matters for how quickly a hospital sees the problem spread. A chance mutation may alter the protein the drug binds to, and if the drug is present that lineage outgrows its neighbours within a few days. Alternatively a ready made resistance gene can travel between cells on a small circular piece of DNA, crossing even between distantly related species, so that a strain becomes resistant without any mutation of its own. Because such pieces often carry several resistance genes together, exposure to one drug can select for organisms that are simultaneously proof against others never used.

Cheese begins when an enzyme preparation clips a specific bond in one of the milk proteins, removing the fragment that keeps the protein clusters apart and allowing them to link into a continuous gel. Cutting the gel releases the watery whey, and the size of the pieces determines how much moisture the resulting curd retains, which is the first decision separating a hard cheese from a soft one. Salt is then added to slow the surviving bacteria and draw out more water. Over the following weeks and months enzymes from the milk, the coagulant and the microbes break down proteins and fats into smaller molecules, and it is these fragments that carry most of the flavour.

A sailing boat can make progress toward the wind because a trimmed sail behaves like a vertical wing rather than a bag being pushed. Air passing the curved leeward side travels farther and faster, the pressure there falls, and the resulting force acts roughly perpendicular to the sail. Most of that force would simply push the hull sideways, but a deep keel or centreboard meets far more resistance moving across the water than along it, so the sideways component is largely resisted and the forward component drives the boat. No boat can sail straight into the wind, so a course upwind is made as a zigzag of alternating slanting legs.

Trees in temperate climates add wood in a thin living layer just under the bark, and the cells formed early in the growing season are wide and thin walled while those formed late are narrow and dense. The abrupt change from dense late wood to the wide cells of the following spring appears in cross section as a line, so counting lines gives the age of the trunk at the height sampled. Ring width varies with growing conditions, and trees in the same region share the pattern of good and poor years. Matching those patterns across overlapping samples lets a sequence be extended backwards well beyond the lifespan of any single tree.

Treating water for a public supply proceeds through stages that each remove a different class of contaminant. A coagulant is stirred in so that fine suspended particles, which are too small to settle and repel one another electrically, clump into flocs heavy enough to sink in a quiet basin. What remains in suspension is caught in a bed of sand and gravel through which the water percolates slowly, and the bed is periodically cleaned by reversing the flow. Finally a disinfectant is added to kill surviving microorganisms, and a residual concentration is deliberately maintained so that the water is still protected while it stands in the pipes of the distribution network.

Pressing a piano key does not push the hammer against the string; it throws it. A train of levers accelerates the hammer, and just before contact a shaped part disengages so the hammer flies the last short distance freely and rebounds immediately, leaving the string free to vibrate. A catch holds the rebounding hammer partway back rather than letting it return the whole distance, which is what allows a note to be repeated rapidly without fully releasing the key. Meanwhile a felt damper that rested on the string has been lifted, and it falls back when the key is released, silencing the note.

A reef is built by colonial animals that secrete a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate beneath their soft tissue, each generation growing on the remains of the last. Inside their cells live single celled algae that photosynthesise and pass most of the sugars they make to the host, which is why the animals thrive in clear, sunlit, nutrient poor water where little else grows abundantly. When water stays too warm for too long the partnership breaks down and the algae are expelled, leaving the tissue pale and the animal dependent on capturing food from the water. If conditions return to normal quickly the algae can be reacquired, but a prolonged episode kills the colony.

Mechanical refrigeration works by moving heat rather than destroying it, using a fluid that changes state at conveniently different pressures. A compressor raises the vapour to a high pressure, which also raises the temperature at which it will condense, and in the outside coil it gives up heat to the room and turns to liquid. The liquid then passes through a narrow restriction into a region of low pressure, where a portion flashes to vapour and the temperature drops sharply. In the inner coil the cold liquid absorbs heat from the cabinet as it boils, and the vapour returns to the compressor to repeat the cycle indefinitely.

No flat map can represent a sphere without distortion, because a curved surface cannot be unrolled onto a plane without stretching or tearing it somewhere, and every projection therefore chooses what to preserve and what to sacrifice. One family keeps angles correct locally, so small shapes look right and a straight line of constant bearing is easy to plot, at the cost of enlarging regions far from the line of contact. Another family keeps areas proportional, which is useful when comparing the extent of regions, but it necessarily skews shapes. A cartographer picks according to the purpose of the map, and a projection chosen for navigation misleads badly when used to compare territories.

Migrating birds appear to combine several independent means of orientation rather than relying on any single one. Experiments in which the apparent position of the sun is shifted show that many species use it as a compass, correcting for its movement through the day with an internal clock. Others raised under artificial skies learn the pattern of rotation of the stars and thereafter fly relative to the point about which the sky turns. There is also good evidence for a sense of the earth's magnetic field, giving direction and perhaps a crude sense of latitude, while landmarks learned on earlier journeys refine the route as an experienced bird approaches a familiar destination.

Smelting iron on a large scale depends less on heat than on chemistry. Ore, coke and limestone are charged into the top of a tall shaft while hot air is blown in near the bottom, and the coke burns to carbon monoxide, which strips oxygen from the iron oxide as the charge descends through progressively hotter zones. The limestone decomposes and combines with the earthy impurities to form a molten slag that floats on the denser metal and can be drawn off separately. The iron that collects at the hearth has dissolved a good deal of carbon from the fuel, making it hard and brittle until that carbon is later removed.

Sound changes in a language tend to be regular: when a sound shifts, it shifts in every word where it occurs in the same surrounding environment, rather than in a scattered handful of words. That regularity is what makes historical reconstruction possible, because correspondences between related languages then form consistent sets rather than random resemblances. A comparison of many such sets allows the sounds of an unrecorded ancestor to be inferred, along with an ordering of the changes that separated the daughters. Words that violate a regular correspondence are often borrowings, and identifying them can reveal contact between speech communities that left no other trace.

Soil forms where rock is broken down by frost, water and acids and the fragments are colonised by organisms whose remains accumulate as organic matter. Over long periods the profile separates into distinguishable layers: a dark upper layer rich in decayed material, a paler layer beneath from which fine clay and dissolved minerals have been washed downward, and a zone lower still where those materials accumulate. The depth and sharpness of these layers depend on rainfall, temperature, the parent rock and the plants growing above. Because the process is slow, soil lost to erosion in a single season may take centuries to replace.

A fission reactor is controlled by exploiting the fact that not every neutron appears at once. Most neutrons are released within a tiny fraction of a second of a nucleus splitting, but a small proportion emerge seconds later from the decay of certain fragments, and it is this delayed group that makes the chain reaction slow enough to steer with mechanical rods. A moderator such as water or graphite slows fast neutrons so they are more readily captured by the fuel, while rods of a strongly absorbing material are inserted or withdrawn to hold the population steady. Coolant flowing past the fuel carries the heat away to raise steam.

On steep ground, cultivation is made possible by cutting the slope into a staircase of level platforms retained by walls of stone or packed earth. Each platform holds water long enough for it to soak in rather than running off, which both feeds the crop and prevents the surface soil from being carried downhill in heavy rain. The walls must be built so that water can drain slowly through them, since a wall that holds water back completely will eventually be pushed over by the pressure behind it. Such systems demand continual repair, and a terrace abandoned for a few seasons often collapses into the one below.

Glass is worked hot because it has no sharp melting point; it merely grows less viscous as the temperature rises, passing gradually from brittle solid to thick, honey like liquid. The worker gathers a mass on the end of a hollow iron rod, shapes it against a wooden block or a metal plate, and inflates it with a breath, reheating whenever the surface stiffens too much to move. Because the outside cools faster than the inside, a finished piece left in the air would develop internal stresses and crack, so it is placed in an oven held near the softening point and cooled over many hours.

Sleep is not uniform but proceeds through repeating cycles of roughly an hour and a half. Early in the night the deeper stages predominate, marked by slow, large electrical waves across the cortex, a low heart rate and a body that is easily moved but hard to wake. Later cycles give more time to a different state in which the brain is active, the eyes move rapidly, and the muscles of the limbs are held almost paralysed. Both kinds appear to matter for retaining what was learned during the day, and a night cut short loses disproportionately much of the state that comes last.

Radio waves reach a distant receiver by more than one path, and which path dominates depends strongly on frequency. Low frequencies follow the curve of the ground, losing energy to the surface but bending well beyond the horizon. Higher frequencies travel in straight lines and are limited to what is visible, unless they meet the electrically charged layers high in the atmosphere, which can refract them back toward the ground and permit contact over thousands of kilometres. Those layers are produced by sunlight and change through the day, so a frequency that carries far after dark may be absorbed entirely at noon.

Whether a volcano erupts quietly or violently depends mainly on how easily gas can escape from the magma. Magma poor in silica is runny, dissolved gas bubbles rise and leave freely, and the result is a flow that spreads over the surrounding land. Magma rich in silica is stiff, bubbles cannot escape, and pressure builds until the rock above fails, at which point the sudden drop in pressure causes the whole mass to expand explosively into fragments. The same reservoir may behave both ways at different times as its composition changes, so the shape of a cone often records a mixed history of flows and ash.

A dictionary entry is not written from the compiler's intuition but assembled from evidence of how a word has actually been used. Examples are gathered from a wide range of writing, sorted, and examined for the recurring patterns that indicate distinct senses, since a sense boundary is a judgement about usage rather than a fact waiting to be discovered. The definition is then drafted so that it fits every example placed under it and excludes those placed elsewhere, using vocabulary simpler than the word being defined. Editors also record the earliest evidence they can find, which is a statement about the surviving record rather than about first use.

When a vessel is cut, bleeding is stopped by two processes working on different timescales. Small fragments circulating in the blood stick to the exposed wall and to each other within seconds, forming a soft plug that is adequate for a minor injury. In parallel a sequence of proteins activates one another in turn, each step amplifying the last, until an enzyme converts a soluble protein into insoluble threads that weave through the plug and bind it into a firm clot. Once the wall beneath has been repaired, a separate enzyme system dissolves the threads, and the balance between the two systems keeps clots local rather than spreading through the circulation.

Turning loose fibre into yarn requires two operations that must be kept in the right order. Drafting pulls a thick rope of fibres out into a thinner strand by passing it between pairs of rollers turning at increasing speeds, so that the fibres slide past one another and the strand attenuates. Twist is then inserted, which presses the fibres together and makes the friction between them great enough to resist being pulled apart. If twist reaches the strand before drafting is complete the fibres lock and the strand will break rather than thin, which is why the machinery is arranged so that twist cannot run back up into the drafting zone.

The sound of a hall depends less on its loudness than on how long sound persists and where the earliest reflections arrive from. A listener hears the direct sound first, then reflections from nearby surfaces, and finally a dense tail as energy bounces many times before being absorbed. Reflections arriving very soon after the direct sound from the side walls make the source seem broad and the hall enveloping, whereas a wide room delivers them late and weak. The overall persistence is set by the volume and by how absorbent the surfaces and the audience are, which is why a hall can sound quite different when it is empty.

Wine begins with yeast converting the sugars of the grape juice into alcohol and carbon dioxide, a process that generates heat and must be cooled if delicate aromas are to survive. Many wines then undergo a second, bacterial conversion in which a sharp acid is changed into a softer one, reducing the acidity and adding a rounder character. Ageing in wooden barrels allows a very slow ingress of oxygen through the staves, which gradually binds the pigment and tannin molecules into larger units that taste less astringent and eventually settle out. The choices at each stage are what distinguish wines made from the same variety in neighbouring vineyards.

A canal crosses a change in ground level through a chamber closed at both ends by gates. A boat travelling upstream enters the chamber at the lower level, the lower gates are shut, and openings in the upper gates are gradually cleared so that water flows in from the reach above until the levels match and the upper gates can swing open. Descending reverses the sequence. Every passage sends a chamber full of water down the flight, so a busy staircase of locks consumes a great deal from the summit level, which must be fed by reservoirs or by pumping water back up.

Photosynthesis is best understood as two linked processes rather than one reaction. Pigments held in stacked membranes absorb light and use the energy to strip electrons from water, releasing oxygen as a by product and driving protons across the membrane; the return flow of those protons powers the synthesis of energy carrying molecules. Those carriers are then spent in a separate cycle of reactions in the surrounding fluid, where carbon dioxide is attached to an existing sugar skeleton and the product is rearranged and reduced to yield a three carbon sugar. Most of that sugar is recycled to regenerate the acceptor, and only a fraction leaves as gain.

An earthquake radiates several kinds of wave that travel at different speeds, and the delay between their arrivals is what allows the source to be located. The fastest is a compression that pushes and pulls the rock along the direction of travel; next comes a shearing motion that displaces the rock sideways and cannot pass through liquid. Slower still are waves confined to the surface, which do most of the damage because they carry large amplitudes and decay gradually with distance. Measuring the interval between the first two arrivals gives the distance to the source from each station, and three or more such distances fix the location.

A sewn book is built from folded sheets rather than single leaves. Several sheets nested together form a gathering, and thread passes through the fold of each gathering and links it to its neighbours, so the pages turn freely and the block opens flat. The spine is then rounded and given a slight shoulder, which helps the volume keep its shape and provides a ledge for the boards to sit against. Boards are attached by tapes or cords carried through from the sewing, and only afterwards is the whole covered in cloth or leather, so that the covering material carries no structural load.

The deep ocean circulates because seawater density depends on both temperature and salt content. Where surface water is chilled and made saltier by the growth of sea ice, it becomes dense enough to sink, and it spreads slowly along the sea floor beneath lighter water. That sinking must be balanced by an equally slow return of water toward the surface elsewhere, aided by mixing driven by winds and tides. A parcel of water leaving the surface may not return for many centuries, which is why measurements of dissolved gases in deep water can be used to estimate how long ago it was last in contact with the atmosphere.

An ant colony behaves as a single reproductive unit, with one or a few egg laying individuals and a large population of workers that do not reproduce. Coordination is achieved almost entirely through chemical signals rather than any central direction: a worker returning from food lays a trail that others follow and reinforce, so a short path is reinforced faster than a long one and quickly dominates. Different chemicals mark the colony's own members, signal alarm, or indicate where the brood should be moved when conditions change. Because each worker follows simple local rules, the colony's apparent planning is a result rather than an instruction.

The efficiency of the early steam engine was crippled by the need to cool the working cylinder in order to condense the steam inside it, then reheat the same metal before the next stroke. Moving the condensation into a separate vessel connected by a valve allowed the cylinder to stay hot throughout, so far less fuel was wasted merely restoring its temperature. The separate vessel could also be kept permanently cold and under partial vacuum, which improved the pressure difference available to drive the piston. This single rearrangement cut fuel consumption dramatically and made engines practical where coal had to be carried a long distance.

Vaccination works by presenting the immune system with a harmless version or fragment of a pathogen so that a response is mounted before any real exposure. The first encounter with a foreign molecule produces antibodies slowly and in modest quantity, but it also leaves behind long lived cells that retain the specificity of that response. If the same molecule appears later, those cells divide rapidly and produce antibodies of higher affinity within days rather than weeks, often clearing the invader before symptoms develop. The durability of that memory varies with the preparation, and some require repeated doses spaced out to raise the response to a lasting level.

A dune forms where wind carrying sand meets an obstacle or a rough patch that slows the flow. Grains do not float in the air but hop, striking the surface and knocking further grains into flight, and this hopping transports material up the gentle windward slope. At the crest the grains fall into the sheltered air beyond and accumulate until the slope grows too steep and slides, producing a steep face whose angle is remarkably consistent. Because sand is removed from the windward side and deposited on the sheltered one, the whole form migrates downwind while keeping its shape, sometimes advancing several metres a year.

A pendulum keeps good time because its period barely depends on the size of its swing, but it will stop unless energy is fed to it, and any feeding disturbs it. The escapement solves both problems by letting a toothed wheel, driven by a weight or spring, advance one tooth per swing while delivering a small push at the moment the pendulum passes its lowest point, where interference with the timing is least. The same intermittent release is what converts continuous drive into the counted steps that the gear train and hands display. A worn escapement gives an uneven push, and the clock's rate then varies with how far the weight has fallen.

The largest whales feed by filtering, using plates of a tough fibrous material that hang from the upper jaw and fray into a mat along their inner edge. Some species swim slowly with the mouth open, letting water pass steadily through the mat while small animals are caught. Others take an enormous gulp, expanding pleated grooves along the throat so the mouth engulfs a volume comparable to the whale's own body, then close the jaws and force the water out through the plates by contracting. Because this method is only worthwhile where prey is densely concentrated, such whales travel long distances to reach the few places where it swarms.

Groundwater is not held in underground rivers but in the pore spaces between grains of sand and gravel or in fractures within rock. What matters for a well is not only how much space exists but how well the spaces connect, since a formation may hold a great deal of water and still yield it too slowly to be useful. Rain soaking in at the surface recharges the store, and the level below which the pores are fully saturated rises and falls with the seasons. Where a permeable layer is confined between impermeable ones and receives water from higher ground, pressure can push water up a borehole without pumping.

Many natural dyes will colour a fibre in the dyebath but wash straight out again, because nothing holds the colouring molecule to the fibre. Treating the material first with a solution of a metal salt leaves metal ions bound to sites along the fibre, and these ions then form a bridge, attaching firmly to the dye molecule at one side and to the fibre at the other. The choice of metal alters the colour as well as the fastness, so a single dye plant can yield a range of shades from yellow through olive to grey depending on the treatment. Fastness to light and to washing are separate properties and do not always improve together.

A moving bicycle stays upright without conscious effort largely because steering the front wheel moves the contact patch under the falling mass. When the machine leans, the front wheel turns into the lean of its own accord, partly because the contact point trails behind the steering axis and partly through the resistance of the spinning wheel to being tilted. The resulting curve carries the wheels back beneath the centre of mass and the lean is corrected. A rider makes larger versions of the same correction, and turning deliberately begins with a brief steer in the opposite direction so that the machine leans the right way.

Most plants do not gather nutrients from the soil alone but through fungal threads that colonise their roots and extend far into the surrounding ground. The threads are far finer than the finest root and reach water and dissolved phosphorus in pores that roots cannot enter, passing much of it to the plant. In exchange the fungus receives sugars, since it cannot photosynthesise for itself, and a substantial share of what a forest fixes moves underground this way. Because a single fungal individual may connect several trees, materials can pass between plants, though how much of this matters to the plants themselves is disputed.

Excavation proceeds on the principle that in undisturbed ground the layers lower down were laid before those above them. Each layer is defined by a change in colour, texture or content rather than by an arbitrary depth, and objects are recorded by the layer they came from, since it is the layer and not the object that carries the sequence. Digging a pit, cutting a ditch or robbing a wall interrupts the sequence and creates a boundary that must be recognised, because material from any earlier layer the pit cut through may be found inside its fill. A single misread boundary can transpose two phases of a site.

Sea salt is produced by letting sunlight and wind do the work of evaporation in a series of shallow ponds connected in sequence. Seawater admitted to the first pond becomes progressively more concentrated as it is moved along, and the least soluble compounds crystallise out early, forming a hard crust on the pond floors that is not harvested. Only when the brine is concentrated to a narrow range does common salt begin to crystallise, and it is raked from the final ponds before the brine reaches the point where bitter magnesium compounds would come out with it. The remaining liquid is discarded to keep those compounds out.

A large telescope mirror is ground to a curve that brings parallel rays to a single focus, which for an unobstructed dish means a shape slightly deeper at the edges than a sphere. Grinding proceeds with progressively finer abrasives, and the surface is tested repeatedly, since an error of a fraction of a wavelength across the whole face is enough to blur the image. The finished glass is not reflective in itself and is coated with a thin metallic film that must be renewed periodically. Because the glass sags under its own weight as the telescope tilts, the mirror rests on a system of supports that spreads the load and adjusts as the orientation changes.

Cattle, sheep and their relatives digest grass by keeping it in a large fermentation chamber ahead of the true stomach. Microorganisms living there produce enzymes the animal itself lacks, breaking the cellulose of plant cell walls into short acids that pass through the chamber wall and supply most of the animal's energy. Material is periodically returned to the mouth and chewed again, reducing its size so the microbes can work on more surface. The microbes are eventually carried onward and digested themselves, providing protein, which is why such animals can thrive on forage far too poor to sustain an animal with a simple stomach.

Where two air masses of different temperature and humidity meet, the boundary between them is a front, and the weather it brings depends on which mass is advancing. When warm air advances it rides gently up over the retreating cold air along a shallow slope, producing a wide band of high cloud that thickens and lowers for many hours before steady rain arrives. When cold air advances it undercuts the warm air steeply, forcing it up quickly into tall clouds and a narrow band of heavy showers that passes rapidly. Since cold fronts move faster, they eventually overtake the warm ones and lift the warm air clear of the surface.

Pottery is normally fired twice for practical rather than aesthetic reasons. The first firing drives off chemically bound water and converts the clay irreversibly into a porous ceramic that is strong enough to handle yet still absorbent, so a glaze suspension applied to it sticks as the water is drawn in. The second firing takes the piece high enough for the glaze to melt into a glassy layer and bond to the body beneath, which requires the two to expand and contract at similar rates or the glaze will craze. Restricting the air supply during firing changes the chemistry of metal oxides in body and glaze, altering colours.

A roundabout replaces the many conflicting paths of a crossroads with a one way circulation that vehicles enter only by merging. Because every entering driver yields to traffic already circulating and nobody crosses an opposing stream, the number of points where paths conflict falls sharply and the remaining conflicts occur at shallow angles and low relative speed. Capacity depends on the gaps available in the circulating flow, so a roundabout works well when the approaching flows are reasonably balanced and poorly when one arm dominates and starves the others. Deflection at entry is deliberately designed in, since a straight approach encourages speeds that defeat the arrangement.

Many seeds do not germinate as soon as they are wet and warm, which prevents a whole crop from sprouting during a mild spell before winter. In some species the coat is impermeable and must be abraded, cracked by frost or partly digested before water can reach the embryo. In others the embryo itself is chemically held back, and the block is lifted only by a prolonged period of cold and damp, so that germination follows a genuine winter rather than a brief cold snap. Some seeds require light and germinate only when brought near the surface, which is why disturbed ground so often produces a flush of seedlings.

An older drainage system carries rain from roofs and streets in the same pipes as household waste, which keeps construction costs down but creates a difficulty in heavy rain. The pipes are sized for a flow far smaller than a storm produces, so relief points are built in that discharge the diluted mixture to a river once the flow exceeds several times its dry weather value. Newer systems separate the two, sending rain directly to a watercourse and waste to treatment. Retrofitting the separation in a built up area is extremely expensive, so much effort goes instead into detaining storm water near where it falls.

A tuning system cannot make every interval acoustically pure, because the pure intervals do not fit together. Stacking twelve pure fifths does not arrive at the note seven octaves above the start but overshoots it slightly, and the small discrepancy has to be absorbed somewhere. Older systems concentrated the error, leaving several keys beautifully in tune and one or two unusable, which gave each key a distinct character. Dividing the octave into twelve equal steps spreads the error evenly instead, making every fifth very slightly narrow and most thirds noticeably wide, but allowing music to move freely between keys without retuning.

A flight feather is a branching structure that behaves as a continuous surface without being one. A central shaft carries a row of branches on each side, and each branch bears smaller branches whose neighbours interlock by means of tiny hooks. Air pressure presses the surface together rather than forcing it apart, and when the surface is torn the bird can zip it closed again by drawing the feather through its bill. Feathers wear and cannot be repaired once grown, so they are replaced periodically, usually a few at a time in matching positions on each side so that flight is not lost.

A metal component may fail under a load it has carried safely thousands of times before, because repeated cycles of stress do cumulative damage that a single application does not. A crack begins at a point of local stress concentration, typically a surface scratch, a sharp internal corner or an inclusion, and advances a minute distance on each cycle, leaving a fracture face marked with fine parallel lines that record the progression. The part carries its load normally until the remaining section is too small, at which point it breaks suddenly. Below a certain stress range some alloys can endure indefinitely, while others accumulate damage at any amplitude.

Limestone caves are dissolved rather than eroded. Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and, more importantly, from decaying matter in the soil, forming a weak acid that reacts with the rock and carries it away in solution along joints and bedding planes. As the passages widen, flow increases and dissolution accelerates, so a few routes come to carry almost all the water while their neighbours are abandoned. Where a solution reaches an air filled chamber it loses carbon dioxide to the air, becomes unable to hold as much dissolved rock, and deposits the excess, building the pendant and mounded formations that grow from ceiling and floor.

A signed language is a full language in its own right and is not a manual rendering of the surrounding spoken one; its grammar can differ completely from that of the spoken language used in the same region. Space carries grammatical work: a signer establishes locations for the people or things under discussion and then directs verbs between those locations to show who acts on whom. Because the hands, face and body can act at once, information that a spoken language must string out in sequence is often expressed simultaneously, with facial movements marking questions, conditions and negation. Signed languages arise wherever deaf people form a community.

Silk is a continuous filament that a moth caterpillar spins around itself as a cocoon, secreting a protein through a small opening and drawing it out into a thread as it moves its head. The filament is coated in a gummy second protein that sticks the coils together. To recover it whole, cocoons are warmed in water to soften the gum, and the loose ends of several are gathered and wound together, since a single filament is too fine to use alone. Because a cocoon that the moth has chewed its way out of yields only short broken lengths, most cocoons are treated before the adult emerges.

Colour vision in most people depends on three kinds of light sensitive cell, each most responsive to a different part of the spectrum, though their ranges overlap broadly. No single cell can report a colour, since a dim light at its best wavelength and a bright light at a poorer one produce the same signal; only the ratio between the responses of different types carries the information. Those responses are recombined early in the visual pathway into signals that represent light against dark, red against green and blue against yellow, which is why certain colour pairs never appear mixed and why staring at a strong colour produces an afterimage in its opposite.

A compost heap works because the microorganisms that break down plant material generate heat faster than a large pile can lose it, so the interior rises well above the surrounding temperature and the process accelerates. The mixture must supply both carbon, from woody or dry material, and nitrogen, from green or wet material, in roughly the ratio the organisms need; too much nitrogen and the surplus escapes as ammonia, too little and decomposition stalls. Air is needed as well, and a heap that becomes waterlogged or is packed too tightly turns sour. Turning the heap restores air and moves the cooler outside material into the hot interior.

Lightning follows the separation of electric charge inside a cloud, which is thought to occur when ice particles of different sizes collide in strong updraughts and exchange charge before being carried to different heights. When the resulting difference becomes large enough to break down the air, a faint channel advances downward in a series of short steps, branching as it goes. As it nears the ground an upward discharge rises to meet it, and once the connection is made a far brighter surge travels back up the established channel. The abrupt heating of the air in that channel makes it expand explosively, and the resulting shock is heard as thunder.
